title: Sichuan Dry-Fried Green Beans
subtitle: Gan bian si ji dou, blistered beans with pork and preserved vegetable
excerpt: Dry-frying drives moisture from the beans until they blister and shrivel, then a quick toss with pork mince, ya cai, and doubanjiang coats every bean in a savoury, slightly spicy sauce. The whole dish takes about 25 minutes. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Gan bian si ji dou (dry-fried four-season beans) is a Sichuan restaurant staple featured in Fuchsia Dunlop's Sichuan Cookery and Land of Fish and Rice. The technique of dry-frying vegetables in a wok with minimal or no oil before adding aromatics appears across Sichuan and Hunan traditions, and the use of Yibin ya cai (Yibin preserved vegetables) as a flavouring agent in this dish is considered the authentic regional approach.

content.text: This serves 4 alongside rice and takes about 25 minutes. The dish relies on a technique called
dry-frying

-- cooking the beans in a very hot wok with almost no oil until they lose their raw moisture and develop blistered, wrinkled skins that grip the sauce. The result is entirely different from steamed or stir-fried beans.

Make sure the beans are completely dry before they go into the wok. Wet beans steam rather than blister, and the batch will take twice as long. Trim both ends and pat with a clean cloth or leave spread on a tray for 10 minutes before cooking.
What you need
Method

Heat the wok over the highest possible flame until it begins to smoke. Add just 5 ml of the oil and swirl to coat. Add the green beans in a single layer -- you may need to do this in two batches depending on wok size. Do not stir for 1 minute to let the underside blister.

Toss the beans and continue dry-frying, stirring every 30 seconds, for a further 5-7 minutes until most of the beans are blistered and slightly shrivelled. They should smell nutty rather than raw. Remove from the wok and set aside.

Add the remaining oil to the wok over high heat. Add the pork mince and break it up with the spatula, cooking until the mince has browned and is beginning to crisp at the edges -- about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 30 seconds, then add the
doubanjiang
. Stir-fry for 1 minute until the paste darkens and the oil turns red.
Add the
ya cai
and stir-fry for 1 minute. The preserved vegetable will release a savoury, slightly funky aroma.
Splash in the
Shaoxing wine
around the edge of the wok so it sizzles on contact. Add the light soy sauce and sugar and stir to combine.

Return the blistered beans to the wok and toss everything together for 2 minutes until the sauce coats every bean. Taste and adjust seasoning -- the dish should be savoury, slightly spicy, and a little sweet. Finish with sesame oil and serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.symptom: Beans are steaming and turning limp rather than blistering
items.cause: The beans were wet or the wok was not hot enough
items.fix: Dry beans thoroughly before cooking and ensure the wok is smoking before the beans go in. If overcrowded, cook in two batches.

items.cause: Ya cai was not rinsed, or doubanjiang varied in salt content
items.fix: Rinse the ya cai before using. Add a pinch of sugar to balance, and reduce any added soy sauce.

items.symptom: The sauce does not cling to the beans
items.cause: Too much oil in the wok, or the beans were not dry enough when returned
items.fix: Drain excess oil before adding the beans back. The sauce should be thick enough to coat without pooling.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Gan bian si ji dou is a Sichuan restaurant staple that appears on virtually every menu in the province. The name translates to 'dry-fried four-season beans' because the dish works with any flat green bean variety grown year round. Ya cai -- preserved, slightly pickled Yibin vegetable -- is the ingredient that sets this dish apart from simpler green bean stir-fries; it adds a distinct fermented depth that the doubanjiang alone cannot replicate. The dish travels well to home kitchens because it benefits from the high-heat wok cooking that domestic hobs can replicate when cleared of other pans.
